picks.style: late antique latin elegy, bowed lyre, low strings, grave male voice, slow processional, restrained lament
picks.why: The closing envoi to the dead teachers — a farewell that stands entirely on its own, ending on memory outliving the ash.

picks.style: roman funeral lament, single flute, muted strings, tenor with chorus response, slow, mournful
picks.why: The solstitial-grass image and the Horace tag 'Nothing is in every part blessed' give it a real turn and a closing line.

picks.style: melancholy urdu ghazal, harmonium, tabla, sarangi, expressive male vocal, rubato, intimate
picks.why: A complete ghazal built on the refrain 'Where now' — Ghalib's great ubi sunt, coherent from first line to last.

picks.style: classical ghazal, sarangi and harmonium, low male voice with slow tabla, brooding, cyclical
picks.why: The 'Again... again...' anaphora returns love, wounds and salt in cycles — made for a repeating musical figure.

picks.style: qawwali-inflected ghazal, harmonium, dholak, handclaps, layered male voices, rising, elegiac
picks.why: Every couplet lands on 'now I am gone' — a posthumous refrain with the momentum of a lament sung after the funeral.

picks.style: late georgian art song, fortepiano, cello, plaintive soprano, unhurried, elegiac
picks.why: Sonnet I entire, closing on the famous line that those paint sorrow best who feel it most.

picks.style: english parlour song, square piano, viola, warm mezzo, slow, resigned
picks.why: A whole sonnet on imagination burning out — self-contained, and the 'robe of flow'rs' image carries it.

picks.style: gothic ballad, minor-key piano, tremolo strings, dramatic soprano, storm-driven, urgent
picks.why: A single unbroken storm-lament over a drowning lover; dramatic voice, lightning, and a refrain-like address to the waters.

picks.style: scots folk song, fiddle, small harp, clear female voice, lilting, plaintive
picks.why: An actual song with a named tune and a repeating 'through the lang muir I'll think o' my Willie' line.

picks.style: georgian parlour air, guitar, gentle female vocal, slow, reflective
picks.why: The beech tree whose leaves revive while the speaker goes down to the grave — the one genuine image in the book.

picks.style: georgian ode, baroque strings and harpsichord, declamatory tenor, stately, gathering
picks.why: Night's dragon-drawn car retreating before the cock-crow — the strongest single image in the collection.

picks.style: english pastoral ode, chamber strings, oboe, warm baritone, moderate, contented
picks.why: The death's-head flag against 'mine be the low and level way' — a clean contrast that a song can turn on.

picks.style: baroque hymn to harmony, organ and strings, choir with soprano solo, radiant, processional
picks.why: Concord chaining the wandering orbs, then riding out on the morning's wings — cosmic and singable.

picks.style: roman satiric elegy, lyre and low flute, wry spoken-sung baritone, measured, dry
picks.why: The one coherent passage among Latin tags and apparatus: Terence courted by nobles, then dying too poor for a hired house.

picks.style: greek tragic chorus, lyre, frame drum, layered female voices, solemn, defiant
picks.why: Antigone's unwritten laws, not of today or yesterday but from all eternity — the most quoted defiance in Greek drama.

picks.style: oracular chant, hollow drone, bone flute, whispered layered voices, slow, ominous
picks.why: A Sibylline prophecy, short and complete, with the built-in cadence of an oracle.
